title: Week 8 · Lesson 24: Dermatologic Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 8 — Lesson 24: Dermatologic Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning

FNP-level goal: Describe a skin finding precisely, connect morphology to pathophysiology, create a safe differential for rash and lesion presentations, recognize skin infection and drug-reaction emergencies, and know when biopsy or dermatology referral is needed.

Learning Objectives

  • Use primary morphology, distribution, timing, symptoms, and exposures to build a differential.
  • Distinguish common inflammatory, infectious, vascular, and neoplastic skin patterns.
  • Recognize red flags for necrotizing soft-tissue infection, severe drug reaction, anaphylaxis/angioedema, vasculitic or purpuric illness, and melanoma concern.
  • Apply safe outpatient-versus-emergency disposition reasoning.

Part 1 — The Skin Is an Immune and Barrier Organ

The epidermis limits water loss and pathogen entry; the dermis contains vessels, nerves, follicles, glands, and immune cells. Barrier disruption, altered microbiome, inflammation, vascular compromise, infection, medication exposure, and neoplasia can all produce “a rash,” but they require very different management.

Start with a description, not a diagnosis: primary lesion, color, blanching, scale, border, configuration, distribution, mucosal involvement, pain versus itch, timing, and systemic findings.

Part 2 — Morphology Creates the Differential

A macule is flat color change; a papule is raised; a plaque is a broader raised lesion; a vesicle contains clear fluid; a pustule contains purulent fluid; a wheal is transient edema; and a bulla is a large blister. Purpura/petechiae represent blood in the skin and do not blanch. Scale, crust, erosion, ulceration, necrosis, and lichenification add diagnostic information.

Distribution matters: flexural versus extensor, dermatomal, acral, sun-exposed, intertriginous, symmetric, localized, generalized, palms/soles, and mucosa. Document morphology in photographs according to policy and patient consent when useful for comparison or consultation.

Part 3 — Inflammatory Disease

Atopic dermatitis reflects barrier dysfunction and type-2 inflammation; itch-scratch cycles can worsen excoriation and secondary infection. Contact dermatitis follows irritant or allergic exposure and often respects exposure pattern. Psoriasis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease that can present with well-demarcated plaques and scale; it is associated with psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic comorbidity.

FNP reasoning: ask about itch, pain, new products, occupation, soaps, plants, metals, medication changes, asthma/allergy history, nail findings, joint symptoms, and infection signs. Avoid calling every erythematous eruption “eczema” or every scale “fungus.”

Part 4 — Infection: Cellulitis, Abscess, and Mimics

Cellulitis is a diffuse infection of skin/subcutaneous tissue; it usually causes warmth, tenderness, erythema, and expanding borders. An abscess is a localized collection and may be fluctuant or drain spontaneously. Source control can be essential for a collection; antibiotics alone may be insufficient.

Common mimics include venous stasis dermatitis, contact dermatitis, DVT, gout, lymphedema, trauma, and inflammatory dermatoses. Bilateral chronic erythema with edema is less typical for acute unilateral cellulitis. Ask whether the diagnosis explains the pain, speed, borders, systemic signs, and portal of entry.

Part 5 — Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection

Necrotizing infection is a rapidly progressive deep infection that can destroy fascia and soft tissue. Early skin findings can be deceptively mild. Pain out of proportion, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, edema beyond erythema, hemorrhagic bullae, ecchymosis, skin anesthesia, crepitus, necrosis, or hypotension are emergency red flags.

Do not delay emergency transfer for office imaging or serial outpatient antibiotics when this process is plausible. The FNP must communicate onset, progression, examination findings, vital signs, host risk factors, and concern for deep infection/sepsis.

Part 6 — Drug Eruptions and SJS/TEN

A medication timeline is essential for a new rash. Many eruptions are benign, but a painful rapidly spreading rash with fever, mucosal erosions, conjunctival symptoms, blistering, skin detachment, facial edema, or systemic illness may represent a severe cutaneous adverse reaction such as SJS/TEN.

Skin pain + mucosal involvement + systemic symptoms after a new medication is an emergency pattern. Stop the suspected medication when clinically appropriate, assess airway and hemodynamic risk, and arrange immediate emergency evaluation. Do not manage suspected SJS/TEN as routine urticaria.

Part 7 — Urticaria, Angioedema, and Anaphylaxis

Urticaria causes transient pruritic wheals from mast-cell mediator release. Angioedema involves deeper tissue swelling. The key question is not whether the rash looks dramatic; it is whether airway, breathing, circulation, or gastrointestinal symptoms suggest anaphylaxis.

Stridor, throat tightness, voice change, tongue/lip swelling with respiratory symptoms, wheeze, hypotension, syncope, or rapidly progressive multisystem symptoms require emergency treatment and transfer. A stable isolated rash may have a different pathway, but must still include a trigger/medication review and return precautions.

Part 8 — Pigmented Lesions and Skin Cancer Reasoning

For a changing pigmented lesion, use the ABCDE framework: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter/evolution. Evolution is especially important. Also assess a nonhealing ulcer, persistent scaly/bleeding lesion, new rapidly enlarging nodule, immunosuppression, prior skin cancer, UV exposure, family history, and full-body skin context.

ABCDE is a triage framework, not a diagnosis. A suspicious lesion needs timely dermoscopy/biopsy or dermatology pathway; do not reassure solely because it is small or painless.

Part 9 — Purpura, Vasculitis, and Systemic Disease

Nonblanching petechiae or purpura may reflect thrombocytopenia, coagulation disorders, vascular inflammation, infection, medication effects, trauma, or embolic disease. Palpable purpura with systemic symptoms can suggest small-vessel vasculitis. Fever plus a rapidly progressive purpuric eruption, toxicity, hypotension, altered mental status, or bleeding requires emergency evaluation.

Connect the skin to the organ system: ask about fever, arthralgia, neuropathy, hematuria, abdominal pain, dyspnea, mucosal bleeding, new medications, infection exposure, and anticoagulants.

Part 10 — Focused Assessment and Diagnostics

History includes onset, progression, itch/pain, fever, contacts, travel, new drugs/supplements, products, occupation, sexual exposure when relevant, immune status, diabetes, vascular disease, prior eruptions, and treatment attempts. Examine the entire relevant skin surface, nails, scalp, mucosa, lymph nodes, pulses, and joints when indicated.

Testing should answer a question: culture purulence when appropriate, microscopy for selected fungal disease, CBC/metabolic testing for systemic illness, ultrasound for a suspected abscess, and biopsy/dermatology referral for uncertain, persistent, atypical, or malignant-appearing lesions. Do not obtain a test that delays emergency disposition for a toxic patient.

Part 11 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 1

A 62-year-old with diabetes develops rapidly increasing leg pain after a minor wound. The erythema expands over hours; there are bullae, HR 118, fever, and pain far beyond the visible margin.

Reasoning: rapid progression, disproportionate pain, bullae, and systemic illness raise concern for necrotizing soft-tissue infection.

FNP decision: emergency transfer now; do not continue a routine cellulitis pathway.

Part 12 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 2

A patient started a new medication 10 days ago and now has fever, malaise, a painful dusky rash, oral erosions, and eye discomfort.

Reasoning: mucosal involvement and painful systemic drug eruption raise concern for SJS/TEN.

FNP decision: urgent emergency evaluation and medication review; this is not uncomplicated contact dermatitis.

Part 13 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 3

A 55-year-old reports a dark lesion that has become asymmetric, multicolored, and larger over several months.

FNP decision: document evolution and arrange timely diagnostic skin evaluation/biopsy pathway. Do not use watchful waiting for an evolving suspicious lesion.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Describe before labeling: morphology + distribution + timing + symptoms + systemic findings.
Infection: distinguish diffuse cellulitis, drainable abscess, and dangerous deep infection.
Medication rash: pain, mucosal disease, blistering, detachment, fever, or systemic symptoms = emergency.
Skin cancer: changing/evolving lesion or nonhealing/bleeding lesion needs diagnostic evaluation.
Emergency transfer: airway involvement, anaphylaxis, sepsis/toxic appearance, necrotizing-infection pattern, severe drug reaction, or rapidly progressive purpura with systemic illness.
